**Short answer:** For an RV that runs a roof air conditioner, the **ALLPOWERS R4000** is the best combination of capacity, solar input, and price in these results. If you want a brand-name unit with a 30A RV port, the **EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3** is the top pick.

## Top picks

| Unit | Capacity | Continuous / surge | Max solar input | Weight | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **ALLPOWERS R4000** | 3,456 Wh | 3,600 W (120 V) / 6,000 W surge | 2,000 W | 45 kg (~99 lb) | Best solar intake and value |
| **EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3** | 4,096 Wh (expandable past 12 kWh) | 4,000 W / 8,000 W | Not stated in these results | Heavy, two-person lift | Full-time boondocking, AC, and home backup |
| **Jackery Explorer 3000 Pro** | 3,024 Wh | 3,000 W / 6,000 W | Not stated in these results | Not stated | Simpler setup for running RV AC |
| **Bluetti AC200L** | 2,048 Wh | 2,400 W / 3,600 W | 1,200 W | ~62 lb | Budget option with a 30A RV port |

Sources: [1], [6], [7]

**ALLPOWERS R4000:** It has three solar inputs at 650 W each, so reaching the full 2,000 W requires panels on all three. Dealectric lists it at $1,499 (list $3,299) on ALLPOWERS's US store, and says a code (EXTRA12) took $179.88 off in a cart test on 2026-10-23. Codes can change, and checkout has the final word. Dealectric earns a commission on purchases through its links.
- Buy link: [ALLPOWERS R4000 via Dealectric](https://dealectric.com/go/allpowers-r4000-3456wh) (affiliate)
- Product page: [dealectric.com/allpowers-r4000-3456wh](https://dealectric.com/allpowers-r4000-3456wh) [1]

**EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3:** Its 4,000 W output and 8,000 W surge are enough to start a 13,500 BTU roof AC (about 1,500 W running, 3,000 W+ on startup). Per the EmergencyEnergy review, one battery runs that AC for roughly 2.3 hours at 85% efficiency. It also reaches 0–80% in about 50 minutes from a wall outlet. Its drawbacks are weight and app-first controls. [6]

**Jackery Explorer 3000 Pro:** The review says its 6,000 W surge handles RV AC starts without a soft-start kit. [6]

**Bluetti AC200L:** It's the budget choice with a built-in 30A RV outlet and a 1,200 W solar ceiling. It's heavier than its capacity suggests. [6][7]

## Solar pairing

- Match the panel array to the unit's solar input ceiling. A 400 W unit won't benefit from more panels, and a 2,000 W unit needs about 2,000 W of panels to use its full input.
- Rooftop arrays are common in RV builds, so check the rated solar input before buying panels. [5]
- I couldn't verify specific solar panel store links in these results. Renogy's 200 W Foldable Solar Suitcase is mentioned as a pairing, but without a source link. [4] Jackery's SolarSaga 100 W and 200 W panels are also mentioned as companion panels. [7]

## Things to check before buying

- **Hookup:** Confirm whether you'll plug into a 30A pedestal or a 15A outlet. A 30A RV outlet (on the Bluetti AC200L and some EcoFlow models) makes shore-power transfer easier. [3][6]
- **Weight:** Most units above 3 kWh need two people or a cart. [6]
- **Conflicting specs:** Sources disagree on some figures. Verify capacity, solar input, and output on the manufacturer's page before buying.
- **Electrical work:** Anything hardwired into the trailer or a home panel needs a licensed electrician. [6]
